FORM: Fashion’s fascination with antiquity reveals as much about the present as the past. What makes a style “classic” and why do particular aesthetics and beauty ideals stand the test of time? Ancient Worlds in Modern Threads brings 20th and 21st century garments into conversation with ancient art and objects across the Mediterranean, focusing on Greece, Rome, and Egypt, exploring how designers reinterpret, reproduce, and reimagine the past through fashion. How do formal elements of design, such as form, shape, line, color, texture, pattern, and point, translate and transform the visual language of antiquity? Tactile and digital experiences invite you to imagine what a display alone cannot convey: the feel of the fabric, the way it moves, and its relation to the living body.

Clothing does more than cover the body; it can change the figure’s proportions and shape through material, structural, and surface elements like folds, layers, and embellishments. The garments presented here invite us to examine how designers use a variety of techniques to create a sense of balance, proportion, rhythm, visual emphasis and aesthetic cohesion.

Dress encompasses clothing, accessories, and other means of altering the physical body, while fashion embodies the changing styles and the meanings attached to them. Change often involves looking back and looking forward. Designers might encounter the ancient world through surviving art objects, later interpretations and reproductions, which in turn shape their reimagining of “classic” or “timeless” styles.

Art Nouveau posters and a 19th century painting inspired by Grecian dress reveal artistic reimaginings of the ancient past. The figures reflect beauty ideals of the artists’ own time, but also carry forward ideals from the ancient world. By looking closely at the garments represented in the artworks, notice how bodies take shape in cloth, and how fabric weight, texture, and movement transform the body form we see.

Actual garments bring these questions into focus through construction and materials. Alongside them, draped terracotta figurines and casts invite you to follow fabric across a shoulder, around a torso, or down a standing figure. Greek and Egyptian vessels and ornaments associated with Egyptomania offer another point of comparison, revealing how decoration frames a surface and draws the eye.

Level T cases explore different ways of shaping the dressed body: Gathers create volume and proportion; Pleats follow the contours of the body form with line, rhythm, and mass; Layers cover and conceal, and Posture affects balance and movement. The exhibition extends upstairs. On Level 1, Ancient World: Greece takes Greek ornament as a starting point for comparing patterns and borders across garments and objects. On Level 2, Ancient World: Egypt explores how color, texture, and reflected light evoke the splendor of ancient Egypt and its enduring appeal to designers.

Look across all of the cases: what similarities and what differences do you notice? Through close looking and comparisons, we can identify what designers preserve and what they change, and begin to hypothesize what their interpretations of the ancient world reveal about their own time and perspectives.
PROXIMITY: Fashion is made to be worn. Fabric bends around the body and refracts light as it responds to the body’s movement. Texture, weight, and shape affect how a garment feels and moves. Historic garments are protected behind glass, preserving them for ongoing study, while keeping many of their material qualities beyond a visitor’s reach.

Other primary source materials contextualize the work. Ralph Rucci’s original sketches lead toward a tactile display on the wall case nearby the Pleats section. Inspired by the fall 1929 textile sample book, tactile pages pair construction drawings with newly made fabric samples. Together with 3D-printed figurines, the object arrangement suggests a path from an idea to a drawing, to experiments with fabric and forms, and finally to a garment. Handle the samples to examine their texture, weight, and structure. Consider how they might interact with the body by touching them with your own hand.

This exhibition is the research site for Designing Proximity: Interactive Strategies for Visitor Engagement in Fashion Exhibitions, a Master of Arts thesis project that explores how tactile and digital tools can help bridge the distance between a museum visitor and the garment or artwork on display. What might handling a fabric sample or rotating a digital model reveal that looking through the glass cannot? What does looking through the glass reveal that a rotating digital model or fabricated facsimile of a textile on display cannot?

The exhibition website extends exploration beyond the boundaries of each case. Scan the QR code on this poster or on labels throughout the exhibition to explore the website and tools that offer partial encounters with the garments: a texture to feel, a detail to enlarge, a model to turn. They cannot recreate the experience of wearing the originals, but they can inspire new questions, curiosities, and understandings. Close-up photographs and rotatable 3D reconstructions reveal details and angles that are difficult to see behind glass, but also may compromise details in the digital rendering process. Compare garments across cases, discover connections beyond the exhibition’s themes, arrange digital objects to create your own exhibition. What would you place together, and why? Your choices can reveal relationships the physical display may not capture.

As part of this research, the curator-researcher will observe visitors’ interactions with the displays and interpretive tools. These observations, combined with visitor feedback will improve current understandings of how tactile and digital experiences contribute to looking at, learning about, and interpreting fashion.
